newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan mutineer has differences with opposition leader.
newsitem.headline: Afghan mutineer has differences with opposition leader.

text.p: General Abdul Malik, whose reported defection to the fundamentalist Islamic Taleban this week broke an 18-month impasse on the frontline in northern Afghanistan, was once an aide to opposition alliance leader Abdul Rashid Dostum.

A senior Taleban official based in the southern city of Kandahar told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) on Tuesday that forces led by Malik had captured Kunduz, capital of Kunduz province, and Sar-i-Pul, the capital of Jowzjan province.
Malik declared support for the Taleban on Monday and said that he had captured 5,000 Dostum soldiers and two provinces, including Faryab to the west of Mazar-i-Sharif.
But opposition spokesman Dr. Abdullah (one name) said on Tuesday that no Taleban forces had yet entered Faryab and that negotiations were going on to try to keep Malik in the opposition alliance.
"So far the Taleban have not entered Faryab. We are trying to solve the problem between Malik and Dostum. We have already started this," said Abdullah.
Malik comes from a powerful family in Afganistan's northern Faryab province. The family was headed by his brother, Rasool Palawan, until his assassination last year.

While Palawan rose to prominence as a military commander under Dostum, Malik was politically active. He became head of foreign relations in the parallel administration that Dostum set up after Afghanistan disintegrated in the wake of the communist defeat in 1992.
During the 1980s, the brothers were part of Dostum's so-called "Uzbek militia", a feared group of irregulars who were aligned with the communist regime.
It was the defection of Dostum and his irregular force in 1992 that allowed the anti-communist mujahiddin to take Kabul.
Dostum's men prevented their erstwhile leader, President Najibullah, from leaving Kabul under a U.N.-brokered deal.
Najibullah spent four years languishing in a U.N. compound in Kabul until the Taleban captured the city last September and killed him.
Shifts in alliances and allegiances have been common in Afghanistan as each commander tries to predict in which direction his greatest personal gain lies.

After the communists fell, Dostum was allied with the faction of President Burhanuddin Rabbani. However, due to a personal conflict between Malik's brother and Rabbani's top military commander, the brothers were not welcome in Kabul.
While the inter-factional conflict raged in Kabul, Palawan consolidated his power in the north, particularly in his native Faryab.
Most of Palawan's men owed their allegiance to him rather than to Dostum. Afghan watchers were speculating that Palawan was preparing to challenge Dostum as the leader of northern Afghanistan.
But Palawan was assassinated in Dostum's stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif last June while Malik was at a United Nations conference in New York.

When he returned from the United States, Malik became leader of his brother's forces and governor of Faryab province. He appeared to have made his peace with Dostum, but he spent less and less time in Mazar-i-Sharif.

An opposition spokesman ascribed Malik's defection to the more recent killing in Mazar-i-Sharif of commander Mullah Abdur Rahman Haqqani and 10 of his bodyguards. The spokesman said that Haqqani was one of Malik's allies.
"Haqqani was one of them. His killing might have provoked this situation," Dr. Abdullah told Reuters.
